catalog_quote: In most polysyllabic roots stress falls on the penultimate syllable. Affixes and clitics are never stressed, nor does affixation ever cause a stress shift. The roots that dont have penultimate stress all have final stress; without exception the presence of a mid vowel in the final syllable causes root-final stress. It should be noted that there is a morpheme structure constraint prohibiting a polysyllsabic morpheme from ending in a mid vowel. Thus, all of these morphemes with a mid vowel in the final syllable have it in a closed syllable. Vowel-final roots virtually always (96%) have penultimate stress. Consonant-final roots which do not have a mid vowel in the final syllable usually (89%) have penultimate stress. audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-hedged: root-penult default, final when the closed final syllable has a mid vowel, (C)VC.CVC roots mostly final, affixes/clitics stress-neutral) rests on the right work -- Nivens 1992, a 100-pp lexical phonology whose first section is 'Stress', and the best description that exists per Glottolog and today's searches -- but only as quoted by StressTyp2 (no page), so the evidence is second-hand. sources.quote: Nivens (1992a:129–37) described the stress patterns of WT. Except for about 10 percent of attested roots which have exceptional final stress, WT stress is root-penultimate unless the final syllable contains a mid vowel, in which case stress must be final.
sources.note: Summary of the author's own 1992 lexical phonology, not a new description. Domain: the root ('root-penultimate'); exceptions: ~10% of attested roots with lexical final stress (matches the catalog's 89% penult); weight: a final syllable containing a mid vowel takes obligatory final stress (p. 119 also states that in WTA, not WTB, no polysyllabic morpheme can end in a mid vowel, so such finals are closed, consistent with the catalog's closed-mid-vowel-final condition; the book's own wording does not mention closure).
